questions.stem: Which act is NOT practice before the IRS?
options: Filing a protest for a client
Appearing as a witness for the taxpayer at the IRS's request
Writing to the IRS about a client's proposed assessment
Rendering written advice on a transaction with potential for tax avoidance
questions.explanation: Section 10.8(b) expressly permits appearing as a witness and furnishing information without it being practice.
questions.pageTitle: What constitutes practice before the IRS

questions.stem: A CPA sends a client a memo on a tax-avoidance arrangement and files nothing. Is she practising before the IRS?
options: No, because nothing was filed
No, until she files a Form 2848
Yes, because rendering such written advice is within the definition
Only if the client acts on the memo
questions.explanation: Section 10.2(a)(4) lists rendering that written advice as a presentation, and § 10.3(b) requires no declaration first.
questions.pageTitle: What constitutes practice before the IRS

questions.stem: An unenrolled preparer completes an entire return for compensation. Which is true?
options: Circular 230 does not apply to him
He must have a PTIN and is subject to subpart B duties and subpart C sanctions
He may represent the client at the resulting examination
He is a practitioner under § 10.2(a)(5)
questions.explanation: Section 10.8(a) imposes both. It does not make him a practitioner or grant representation rights.
questions.pageTitle: What constitutes practice before the IRS

questions.stem: Which of these has unlimited representation rights before the IRS?
options: An Annual Filing Season Program participant
An enrolled retirement plan agent
An enrolled agent
A PTIN holder with no credential
questions.explanation: Only attorneys, CPAs, and enrolled agents may represent any client on any matter.
questions.pageTitle: Who may practice before the IRS, and how far their rights extend

questions.stem: An Annual Filing Season Program participant prepared and signed a client's return. The case is going to Appeals. May she represent the client there?
options: Yes, because she prepared and signed the return
No — her rights stop at revenue agents, customer service, and similar employees
Yes, if she obtains a Form 2848
Yes, if the client also attends
questions.explanation: Limited rights exclude appeals and collection even for a return she prepared and signed.
questions.pageTitle: Who may practice before the IRS, and how far their rights extend

questions.stem: Which individual may NOT represent the taxpayer under § 10.7(c)(1)?
options: A regular full-time employee representing her corporate employer
A general partner representing the partnership
A part-time contractor representing the company that engaged him
An individual representing his spouse
questions.explanation: The category requires a bona fide officer or a regular full-time employee; a contractor is neither.
questions.pageTitle: Who may practice before the IRS, and how far their rights extend

questions.stem: An executor is handling a decedent's final return. What authorises him to deal with the IRS?
options: Form 2848, because he represents the estate
Nothing — an executor may not deal with the IRS
He is treated as the taxpayer under § 10.7(e), so a fiduciary notice applies rather than a power of attorney
Form 8821
questions.explanation: Section 10.7(e) treats a fiduciary as the taxpayer, not as a representative.
questions.pageTitle: Who may practice before the IRS, and how far their rights extend

questions.stem: A practitioner may decline to submit requested records where:
options: The client instructs them not to
They believe in good faith and on reasonable grounds that the records are privileged
A fee dispute is outstanding
The request is inconvenient
questions.pageTitle: Information to be furnished to the IRS

questions.stem: Records are held by neither the practitioner nor the client. The practitioner must:
options: Obtain them from the third party
Notify the IRS promptly, supply what they know about who holds them, and make reasonable inquiry of the client
Do nothing further
Independently verify the client's account
questions.explanation: Section 10.20(a)(2) requires inquiry of the client only.
questions.pageTitle: Information to be furnished to the IRS

questions.stem: OPR asks a practitioner about a colleague's alleged Circular 230 violation. The practitioner:
options: May decline as it does not concern their own client
Must provide the information and testify in any proceeding instituted under the part
Must provide information but need not testify
May respond only under summons
questions.explanation: Section 10.20(a)(3).
questions.pageTitle: Information to be furnished to the IRS

questions.stem: IRC 7525 privilege does not apply to:
options: Non-criminal tax matters before the IRS
Communications concerning tax shelters
Communications with an enrolled agent
Non-criminal federal court proceedings
questions.pageTitle: Information to be furnished to the IRS

questions.stem: A practitioner asserts blanket privilege over an entire file without considering its contents, to delay an examination. This:
options: Is protected by § 10.20(a)(1)
Breaches § 10.20 and may also breach § 10.20(b)'s bar on interference
Is a matter for the client alone
Is permitted if the client agrees
questions.pageTitle: Information to be furnished to the IRS

questions.stem: A practitioner learns a client omitted income from a prior year's return. Circular 230 requires the practitioner to:
options: Notify the IRS
Advise the client promptly of the omission and of its consequences under the Code
File an amended return
Withdraw from the engagement
questions.explanation: Section 10.21.
questions.pageTitle: Omission or error on return, document, or affidavit

questions.stem: The client, properly advised, refuses to correct the error. The practitioner has:
options: Breached Circular 230
Complied with § 10.21; what follows depends on whether continuing would assist the noncompliance
A duty to report the refusal
A duty to resign immediately
questions.pageTitle: Omission or error on return, document, or affidavit

questions.stem: Advising the client of "the consequences" means:
options: Mentioning that an amendment may be needed
Explaining the consequences under the Code and regulations — tax, interest, applicable penalties, and where relevant the absence of a limitation period
Quantifying the exact liability
Providing a written opinion
questions.pageTitle: Omission or error on return, document, or affidavit

questions.stem: A practitioner discloses a client's uncorrected error to the IRS without authority. This:
options: Is required by § 10.21
Risks criminal liability under IRC § 7216 and civil liability under § 6713
Is protected by Circular 230
Is required only for fraud
questions.pageTitle: Omission or error on return, document, or affidavit

questions.stem: Which provision engages if the practitioner goes on to help the client continue the noncompliance?
options: Section 10.21 alone
Section 10.20
Section 10.23
questions.pageTitle: Omission or error on return, document, or affidavit

questions.stem: A former revenue officer had official responsibility for a collection matter during her final six months at the IRS but never worked it personally. She left in June 2026. When may she represent that taxpayer in that matter?
options: Immediately
After June 2027
After June 2028
Never
questions.explanation: Section 10.25(b)(3) imposes a two-year bar where the former employee had official responsibility within one year prior to termination.
questions.pageTitle: Rules for employing or accepting assistance from former IRS employees or disbarred/suspended persons

questions.stem: A former IRS attorney personally and substantially participated in a particular matter involving specific parties. His new firm wishes to represent one of those parties in that matter. What must the firm do?
options: Nothing; the bar is personal to the attorney
Isolate him and execute a sworn statement under § 10.25(c)(2)
Obtain the client's written consent
Wait two years from his departure
questions.explanation: Section 10.25(c)(1) bars firm members unless the firm isolates the former employee, and § 10.25(c)(2) requires a statement under oath by him and another member of the firm, retained and produced to the IRS on request.
questions.pageTitle: Rules for employing or accepting assistance from former IRS employees or disbarred/suspended persons

questions.stem: Which of the following is not a "government employee" for purposes of Circular 230 § 10.25?
options: A member of a State legislature
An employee of the District of Columbia
A special Government employee under 18 U.S.C. § 202(a)
An employee of a foreign tax administration
questions.explanation: Section 10.25(a)(2) covers officers and employees of the United States and its agencies, special Government employees, the District of Columbia, any State, and members of Congress or of a State legislature.
questions.pageTitle: Rules for employing or accepting assistance from former IRS employees or disbarred/suspended persons

questions.stem: An enrolled agent unknowingly engages a research contractor who is under suspension from practice before the IRS. Has the enrolled agent violated § 10.24?
options: Yes, the section imposes strict liability
Yes, because the assistance was indirect
No, because § 10.24 requires the practitioner to act knowingly
No, because research is never practice before the IRS
questions.explanation: Section 10.24 opens "A practitioner may not, knowingly and directly or indirectly." Diligence questions under §§ 10.22 and 10.36 may still arise.
questions.pageTitle: Rules for employing or accepting assistance from former IRS employees or disbarred/suspended persons

questions.stem: For how long is a former government employee barred from communicating with Treasury with intent to influence the interpretation of a rule they helped develop?
options: Six months
One year after government employment ends
Two years after government employment ends
Permanently
questions.explanation: Section 10.25(b)(4), which does not preclude appearing on one's own behalf or representing a taxpayer in a particular matter involving specific parties applying that rule, provided no confidential information from the rule's development is used or disclosed.
questions.pageTitle: Rules for employing or accepting assistance from former IRS employees or disbarred/suspended persons

questions.stem: Which description may an enrolled agent use?
options: "Certified enrolled agent"
"Enrolled to practice before the Internal Revenue Service"
"IRS-authorized tax representative"
"Certified by the Internal Revenue Service"
questions.explanation: Section 10.30(a)(1) supplies this as an acceptable description, bars the term "certified," and bars any description implying an employer/employee relationship with the IRS.
questions.pageTitle: Rules for restrictions on advertising, solicitation and fee information

questions.stem: A practitioner publishes a fee schedule continuously on his website from 4 January until he removes it on 30 September. Through what date must he honour the published rates?
options: 3 February, 30 days after first publication
At least 30 October, 30 days after the last date of publication
Only while the schedule is displayed
For 36 months from first publication
questions.explanation: Section 10.30(b)(2) measures at least 30 calendar days from the last date on which the schedule was published.
questions.pageTitle: Rules for restrictions on advertising, solicitation and fee information

questions.stem: Which is not a category of fee information a practitioner may disseminate under § 10.30(b)(1)(i)?
options: Hourly rates
Fixed fees for specific routine services
A percentage of the tax savings obtained
The fee charged for an initial consultation
questions.explanation: The four listed categories are fixed fees for specific routine services, hourly rates, range of fees for particular services, and the initial consultation fee. A percentage of savings would also engage the contingent-fee prohibition of § 10.27.
questions.pageTitle: Rules for restrictions on advertising, solicitation and fee information

questions.stem: A practitioner runs television advertisements. What must be retained, and for how long?
options: The script, for 12 months
A recording of the actual transmission, for at least 36 months from the last transmission
The media invoice, for 3 years from first broadcast
Nothing, retention applies only to direct mail
questions.explanation: Section 10.30(c) requires the broadcast to be recorded and the recording of the actual transmission retained for at least 36 months from the date of the last transmission or use.
questions.pageTitle: Rules for restrictions on advertising, solicitation and fee information

questions.stem: Is an uninvited written solicitation of employment in an IRS matter prohibited by Circular 230?
options: Yes, in all cases
Yes, unless the recipient is an existing client
Only where it violates Federal or State law or another applicable rule
Only where it discloses fee information
questions.explanation: Section 10.30(a)(2) is conditional. Any lawful solicitation must still clearly identify itself as a solicitation and, if applicable, identify the source of the information used in choosing the recipient.
questions.pageTitle: Rules for restrictions on advertising, solicitation and fee information

questions.stem: A contingent fee is permitted for services in connection with:
options: Preparing an original return claiming a large refund
The IRS's examination of or challenge to an original return
Any amended return
Tax planning advice
questions.pageTitle: Fee rules (e.g., contingent, unconscionable)

questions.stem: A practitioner charges a fixed fee and agrees to refund it if the IRS successfully challenges the position. This is:
options: Permitted, the fee being fixed
A contingent fee, because the practitioner reimburses the client if the position is not sustained
Permitted if disclosed in writing
An unconscionable fee
questions.explanation: Section 10.27(c)(1).
questions.pageTitle: Fee rules (e.g., contingent, unconscionable)

questions.stem: The 120-day period in § 10.27(b)(2)(ii) runs from:
options: The filing of the amended return
The taxpayer's receipt of written notice of the examination of, or challenge to, the original return
The start of the examination
The due date of the original return
questions.pageTitle: Fee rules (e.g., contingent, unconscionable)

questions.stem: A contingent fee is permitted for a claim for refund filed solely in connection with:
options: A disputed deduction
The determination of statutory interest or penalties assessed by the IRS
A carryback
An amended return filed at any time
questions.explanation: Section 10.27(b)(3).
questions.pageTitle: Fee rules (e.g., contingent, unconscionable)

questions.stem: Having published a schedule of fees, a practitioner may charge no more than the published rates for:
options: 7 days
At least 30 calendar days after the last publication date
One year
The remainder of the tax year
questions.pageTitle: Fee rules (e.g., contingent, unconscionable)

questions.stem: Circular 230 § 10.22 requires due diligence in:
options: Preparing returns only
Preparing, approving and filing papers; determining the correctness of representations to Treasury; and determining the correctness of representations to clients
Written advice only
Determining eligibility for refundable credits
questions.pageTitle: Due diligence requirements

questions.stem: A practitioner relies on a subordinate's work product. The presumption of diligence applies if the practitioner:
options: Reviews the final output
Used reasonable care in engaging, supervising, training and evaluating the person, taking proper account of the relationship
Obtains the subordinate's written confirmation
Is not personally aware of any error
questions.explanation: Section 10.22(b).
questions.pageTitle: Due diligence requirements

questions.stem: The reliance presumption is expressly modified by:
options: Sections 10.20 and 10.21
Sections 10.34 and 10.37
Section 10.51
No other section
questions.pageTitle: Due diligence requirements

questions.stem: A practitioner tells a revenue agent something inaccurate, honestly believing it, without checking. This:
options: Is outside § 10.22, which governs returns
Engages § 10.22(a)(2), which requires diligence in determining the correctness of representations to Treasury
Is excused by the honest belief
Engages § 10.21
questions.pageTitle: Due diligence requirements

questions.stem: Section 10.22 may be violated recklessly or through gross incompetence:
options: Yes, like §§ 10.34 to 10.37
No; it is not listed in § 10.52(a)(2), so a violation must be willful
Only in written advice
Only where a penalty results
questions.pageTitle: Due diligence requirements

questions.stem: A practitioner obtains oral informed consent from both affected clients on 3 March and sends the written confirmations on 8 April. Is the § 10.29(b) exception available?
options: Yes, because consent was obtained before the representation began
Yes, if the delay was reasonable
No, because the confirmation came later than 30 days after the informed consent
No, because oral informed consent is never sufficient
questions.explanation: Section 10.29(b)(3) permits written confirmation within a reasonable period after informed consent but in no event later than 30 days.
questions.pageTitle: Conflict of interest

questions.stem: Does a conflict arising from the practitioner's responsibilities to someone who is not and never was a client fall within § 10.29?
options: No, the section applies only between current clients
Yes, if there is a significant risk the representation will be materially limited
Only if the third person is a party to the same matter
Only where the third person pays the fee
questions.explanation: Section 10.29(a)(2) reaches responsibilities to another client, a former client or a third person, and personal interests of the practitioner.
questions.pageTitle: Conflict of interest

questions.stem: A representation begins in January 2026 and concludes in November 2027. From what date does the 36-month retention period for the written consents run?
options: January 2026, the date of the consents
The date the return was filed
November 2027, the conclusion of the representation
The date the IRS closes the case file
questions.explanation: Section 10.29(c) measures the period from the date of the conclusion of the representation of the affected clients.
questions.pageTitle: Conflict of interest

questions.stem: Both affected clients sign thorough, fully informed written waivers, but the practitioner privately doubts he can advocate properly for the second client. May he proceed?
options: Yes, the written waivers satisfy § 10.29(b)
Yes, if he discloses the doubt in writing
No, because § 10.29(b)(1) requires his own reasonable belief that he can represent each client competently and diligently
No, because conflicts of this kind are prohibited by law
questions.explanation: The three conditions of § 10.29(b) are cumulative and (b)(1) is not the clients' to waive.
questions.pageTitle: Conflict of interest

questions.stem: What mental state must the IRS establish to sanction a practitioner for violating § 10.29?
options: Negligence
Recklessness or gross incompetence
Wilfulness
Strict liability, no mental state required
questions.explanation: Section 10.52(a)(1) reaches wilful violation of any regulation in Part 10 other than § 10.33; § 10.29 is not among the sections named in the reckless-or-gross-incompetence limb of § 10.52(a)(2).
questions.pageTitle: Conflict of interest

questions.stem: Which of the following may a representative holding a Form 2848 power of attorney not do?
options: Sign a closing agreement
Sign a consent extending the period of limitations on assessment
Endorse or negotiate the taxpayer's refund check
Sign a waiver of restrictions on assessment of a deficiency
questions.explanation: Circular 230 § 10.31(a) prohibits it, and IRC § 6695(f) penalises it where the practitioner prepared the return; a power of attorney does not confer the authority.
questions.pageTitle: Rules for refund check negotiation

questions.stem: A preparer enters the firm's own bank account on the direct-deposit line of a client's return, with the client's written permission. Which is correct?
options: Permitted, because the client consented in writing
Permitted, because no paper check was endorsed
Prohibited, because directing payment electronically into an account owned by the practitioner's firm is negotiation
Prohibited only if the preparer deducts a fee
questions.explanation: Section 10.31(a) expressly includes directing payment by any means, electronic or otherwise, into an account owned or controlled by the practitioner or an associated firm. Neither section contains a consent exception.
questions.pageTitle: Rules for refund check negotiation

questions.stem: A preparer affixes the taxpayer's name to a refund check, with the taxpayer's authorisation, to deposit it into an account held jointly by the taxpayer and the preparer. Is the deposit within the Reg. § 1.6695-1(f)(1) carve-out?
options: Yes, because the taxpayer authorised it
Yes, because the taxpayer is an account holder
No, because the carve-out excludes joint accounts that include the tax return preparer
No, because the carve-out applies only to electronic refunds
questions.explanation: The regulation permits a joint account of the taxpayer and one or more other persons excluding the tax return preparer.
questions.pageTitle: Rules for refund check negotiation

questions.stem: Which condition is not required for the bank exception in IRC § 6695(f)?
options: The bank deposits the full amount of the check
The deposit is to the taxpayer's account for the taxpayer's benefit
The bank has made a loan to the taxpayer based on the anticipated refund
The bank does not initially endorse or negotiate the check
questions.explanation: A refund-anticipation loan defeats the exception rather than being required by it — Reg. § 1.6695-1(f)(2)(i).
questions.pageTitle: Rules for refund check negotiation

questions.stem: Which statement about the scope of Circular 230 § 10.31 as amended in 2014 is correct?
options: It applies only to practitioners who prepare tax returns
It applies to any practitioner, whether or not they prepare returns
It applies only to paper refund checks
It applies only to accounts owned personally by the practitioner
questions.explanation: T.D. 9668 removed the "who prepares tax returns" limitation and added the electronic parenthetical reaching accounts owned or controlled by the practitioner or an associated firm or entity.
questions.pageTitle: Rules for refund check negotiation

questions.stem: Which standard governs a position taken on a tax return under Circular 230 § 10.34?
options: The position must not be frivolous
The position must not lack a reasonable basis, and must not be an unreasonable position under IRC § 6694(a)(2)
The position must be more likely than not to succeed
The position must have substantial authority in all cases
questions.explanation: Section 10.34(a)(1) uses reasonable basis and the § 6694(a)(2) standards; "not frivolous" is the document standard in § 10.34(b).
questions.pageTitle: Standards for written advice, covered opinions, tax return positions and preparing returns

questions.stem: What happened to the covered opinion rules?
options: They were moved to § 10.37 unchanged
They were repealed by T.D. 9668 effective June 12, 2014, and § 10.35 now addresses competence
They apply only to listed transactions
They were codified in IRC § 6694
questions.explanation: The 2014 amendments removed the covered opinion regime and replaced it with a single principles-based written-advice standard in § 10.37.
questions.pageTitle: Standards for written advice, covered opinions, tax return positions and preparing returns

questions.stem: Must a practitioner advise a client of penalties where the practitioner faces no penalty exposure of their own?
options: No, the duty is tied to the practitioner's own exposure
Only if the client asks
Yes, § 10.34(c)(3) applies the duty regardless
Only for positions the practitioner personally signed
questions.explanation: Section 10.34(c)(3) applies even if the practitioner is not subject to a penalty with respect to the position or paper, and the duty extends to disclosure opportunities and adequate disclosure requirements.
questions.pageTitle: Standards for written advice, covered opinions, tax return positions and preparing returns

questions.stem: Which may a practitioner take into account in giving written advice?
options: The likelihood the return will not be audited
The likelihood the issue will not be raised
The scope of the engagement and the specificity of the advice sought
The client's history of never being examined
questions.explanation: Section 10.37(c)(1) makes scope and specificity part of the reasonable practitioner standard; § 10.37(a)(2)(vi) forbids weighing audit risk.
questions.pageTitle: Standards for written advice, covered opinions, tax return positions and preparing returns

questions.stem: When must a practitioner make reasonable inquiries of a client under § 10.34(d)?
options: Always, before signing any return
Where the information appears incorrect, inconsistent with an important fact or another assumption, or incomplete
Only where the client has been examined before
Never; good faith reliance is absolute
questions.explanation: Reliance in good faith without verification is the general rule, but the practitioner may not ignore the implications of information furnished or actually known.
questions.pageTitle: Standards for written advice, covered opinions, tax return positions and preparing returns

questions.stem: An enrolled agent completes 24, 24 and 24 hours across the three enrollment years of a cycle, with six ethics hours all taken in the final year. Has she satisfied § 10.6(e)(2)?
options: Yes, the cycle total and the ethics total are both met
No, because two ethics hours are required in each enrollment year
No, because 72 hours is a minimum and she completed exactly 72
Yes, because ethics hours may be taken at any time in the cycle
questions.explanation: Section 10.6(e)(2)(ii) requires a minimum of 16 hours including two hours of ethics or professional conduct during each enrollment year.
questions.pageTitle: Continuing education requirements

questions.stem: How many contact hours does a standalone 90-minute program yield?
options: Two
One and a half
One
Zero
questions.explanation: Section 10.6(g)(2) grants credit only for a full contact hour of 50 minutes or multiples of it; a program of more than 50 but less than 100 minutes counts as one.
questions.pageTitle: Continuing education requirements

questions.stem: An individual receives initial enrolment with eight months remaining in an enrollment cycle, touching two enrollment years. What is required?
options: 72 hours including six ethics hours
16 hours including two ethics hours
16 hours including four ethics hours
24 hours including two ethics hours
questions.explanation: Two hours per month enrolled under § 10.6(e)(2)(iii)(A) gives 16 hours, and two ethics hours per enrollment year touched under § 10.6(e)(2)(iii)(B) gives four.
questions.pageTitle: Continuing education requirements

questions.stem: For how long must an enrolled agent retain continuing education records?
options: Three years from the date of the program
Four years following the date of renewal
Three years following the close of the enrollment cycle
Six years from renewal
questions.explanation: Section 10.6(h)(1) requires retention for four years following the date of renewal.
questions.pageTitle: Continuing education requirements

questions.stem: An enrolled agent placed in inactive status completes the missing hours and files for reinstatement. May those hours also count toward the cycle in which she returns to active status?
options: Yes, hours count in the year completed
Yes, if taken in that cycle
No, § 10.6(j)(5) bars using them for the cycle in which she is placed back on the active roster
Only the ethics hours may be counted twice
questions.explanation: Section 10.6(j)(5) provides that credit used for reinstatement may not be used to satisfy the requirements of the enrollment cycle in which the individual is placed back on the active roster.
questions.pageTitle: Continuing education requirements

questions.stem: Which standard does IRC § 6662(d)(2)(C)(ii) use in defining a tax shelter?
options: The sole purpose is tax avoidance
The principal purpose is tax avoidance
A significant purpose is the avoidance or evasion of Federal income tax
The arrangement lacks economic substance
questions.explanation: The Taxpayer Relief Act of 1997 substituted "a significant purpose" for "the principal purpose," so an arrangement with real business purpose can still be a tax shelter.
questions.pageTitle: Tax shelters

questions.stem: Which two conditions must both be met for a person to be a material advisor under IRC § 6111?
options: Signing the return and deriving any fee
Providing material aid, assistance or advice as to the transaction, and deriving gross income above the threshold amount
Promoting the transaction and holding a PTIN
Filing a § 6112 list and deriving gross income above the threshold
questions.explanation: Section 6111(b)(1)(A) requires both the conduct prong and the gross-income prong; the conduct prong covers organizing, managing, promoting, selling, implementing, insuring or carrying out the transaction.
questions.pageTitle: Tax shelters

questions.stem: Must a material advisor who is not required to file a § 6111 return still maintain a § 6112 list?
options: No, the list follows the return requirement
Yes, § 6112(a) applies whether or not a § 6111 return is required
Only for listed transactions
Only if the Secretary requests it in advance
questions.explanation: The parenthetical in § 6112(a) says so expressly. The list is maintained, made available on written request, and retained for the statutory period.
questions.pageTitle: Tax shelters

questions.stem: What distinguishes a listed transaction from another reportable transaction?
options: A listed transaction involves a partnership
A listed transaction is one the Secretary has specifically identified as a tax avoidance transaction, or one substantially similar to it
A listed transaction always involves a material advisor
A listed transaction is disclosed on a different form
questions.explanation: Section 6707A(c)(2). The distinction drives substantially larger penalties under both § 6707A and § 6707.
questions.pageTitle: Tax shelters

questions.stem: What determines when an enrolled agent's renewal window falls?
options: The date of initial enrolment
The last digit of the individual's Social Security or tax identification number
The date the enrollment card expires
The individual's choice at initial enrolment
questions.explanation: Section 10.6(d)(2) groups agents by last digit — 0–3, 4–6, and 7–9 — and (d)(2)(v) carries each group forward every third year.
questions.pageTitle: Enrollment cycle and renewal

questions.stem: An enrolled agent renews between November 1 and January 31. When is the renewal effective?
options: Immediately on filing
January 31
April 1, the first day of the fourth month after the renewal period closes
On the date the IRS issues the card
questions.explanation: Section 10.6(e)(1)(iv) defines the effective date of renewal as the first day of the fourth month following the close of the renewal period.
questions.pageTitle: Enrollment cycle and renewal

questions.stem: Within what period must an enrolled agent notify the IRS of a change of address under Circular 230?
options: 30 days
60 days
90 days
At the next renewal
questions.explanation: Section 10.6(c). That notification does not change the practitioner's last known address for IRC § 6212 purposes.
questions.pageTitle: Enrollment cycle and renewal

questions.stem: An enrolled agent has been on the inactive roster for three years and eight months without renewing. What is his status?
options: Still inactive and eligible to reinstate by renewal
Automatically reinstated
Terminated; eligibility must be re-established from the beginning
Suspended under subpart D
questions.explanation: Section 10.6(j)(6) removes the individual from the inactive roster and terminates the status where renewal is not filed and the requirements satisfied within three years of being placed in inactive status.
questions.pageTitle: Enrollment cycle and renewal

questions.stem: May an individual who is the subject of a pending disciplinary matter elect inactive retirement status?
options: Yes, at any time
Yes, with the consent of the Office of Professional Responsibility
No, § 10.6(k) makes it unavailable in that case
Only after the matter is referred to an administrative law judge
questions.explanation: Section 10.6(k) makes inactive retirement status unavailable to an individual who is ineligible to practise or who is the subject of a pending disciplinary matter; § 10.6(j)(7) does the same for inactive status.
questions.pageTitle: Enrollment cycle and renewal

questions.stem: Circular 230 § 10.23 prohibits a practitioner from:
options: Delaying a matter beyond 30 days
Unreasonably delaying the prompt disposition of any matter before the IRS
Any delay whatever
Delaying only in collection matters
questions.pageTitle: Rules for prompt disposition of matters before the IRS

questions.stem: A practitioner delays because the client instructs him to, hoping the collection statute will expire. This is:
options: Permissible, the client's instruction governing
A violation of § 10.23, and the instruction is no defence
Permissible if disclosed to the IRS
A matter for the client alone
questions.pageTitle: Rules for prompt disposition of matters before the IRS

questions.stem: Section 10.23 may be violated:
options: Recklessly or through gross incompetence, like §§ 10.34 to 10.37
Only willfully, since § 10.52(a)(2) does not list it
Without any mental state
Only where actual harm results
questions.pageTitle: Rules for prompt disposition of matters before the IRS

questions.stem: An enrolled agent misses deadlines through genuine illness, then contacts the examiner and agrees a revised schedule. This is:
options: A violation, deadlines having been missed
Not unreasonable delay
A violation unless the IRS agrees in writing
A violation of § 10.20
questions.pageTitle: Rules for prompt disposition of matters before the IRS

questions.stem: A practitioner advises a client to file a paper whose purpose is to postpone collection. Beyond § 10.23, this engages:
options: Section 10.20(a)
Section 10.34(b)(2)(i), and potentially IRC § 6702 for the client
Section 10.28
Section 10.31
questions.pageTitle: Rules for prompt disposition of matters before the IRS

questions.stem: A client requests their records during a fee dispute. The practitioner:
options: May retain everything until paid
Must generally return records necessary for the client to comply with federal tax obligations, a fee dispute not relieving the responsibility
Must return everything including their own work product
May retain records for 30 days
questions.explanation: Circular 230 § 10.28(a).
questions.pageTitle: Rules for returning a client's records and documents

questions.stem: Where state law permits retention during a fee dispute, the practitioner must still:
options: Return everything
Return records that must be attached to the return, and give reasonable access to review and copy the rest
Do nothing further
Return records only after 90 days
questions.pageTitle: Rules for returning a client's records and documents

questions.stem: Which is a "record of the client" under § 10.28(b)?
options: A depreciation schedule the practitioner prepared, withheld pending payment
Bank statements the client provided
A draft return prepared by the practitioner's employee, withheld pending payment
The practitioner's engagement notes
questions.pageTitle: Rules for returning a client's records and documents

questions.stem: An appraisal prepared by an independent appraiser and provided during the representation is:
options: The practitioner's work product
A record of the client, the appraiser not being the practitioner's employee or agent
Excluded because the practitioner engaged the appraiser
Returnable only if the client paid the appraiser
questions.pageTitle: Rules for returning a client's records and documents

questions.stem: After returning the client's records, the practitioner:
options: May not keep copies
May retain copies, and separately must keep a copy or list for three years under IRC § 6107(b)
Must destroy the file
Must obtain the client's consent to keep copies
questions.pageTitle: Rules for returning a client's records and documents

questions.stem: Must an enrolled agent who prepares no returns for compensation obtain a PTIN?
options: No, the requirement attaches only to preparation
Yes, every enrolled agent must obtain and renew one
Only if the agent represents taxpayers in examinations
Only in a renewal year
questions.explanation: The IRS guidance states a PTIN must be obtained by all enrolled agents, and Circular 230 § 10.6(d)(2)(i) requires every enrolled agent to renew it as prescribed.
questions.pageTitle: PTIN requirements

questions.stem: Which factor is not listed in Reg. § 1.6109-2(g) for "all or substantially all"?
options: Complexity of the work relative to the return's overall complexity
Amount of income, deductions or losses attributable to the work
Hours spent relative to total preparation time
Amount of tax or credit attributable to the work
questions.explanation: The regulation lists complexity, amounts of items, and amount of tax or credit; hours worked is not a factor.
questions.pageTitle: PTIN requirements

questions.stem: Which act may an uncredentialed individual with no PTIN perform for compensation under § 10.8(b)?
options: Sign a return as paid preparer
Prepare less than substantially all of a return
Represent a taxpayer in an examination
Prepare all of a simple return
questions.explanation: Section 10.8(b) permits preparing less than substantially all of a return, appearing as a witness, and furnishing information at the IRS's request.
questions.pageTitle: PTIN requirements

questions.stem: Three preparers in one office file all returns under the senior preparer's PTIN. Permitted?
options: Yes, if he reviews every return
Yes, if the firm's EIN also appears
No, each individual who prepares for compensation must have their own PTIN
Yes, for returns he signs
questions.explanation: Each preparer must have his or her own PTIN and may hold only one; Reg. § 1.6109-2(a)(1) requires the number of the preparer required to sign.
questions.pageTitle: PTIN requirements

questions.stem: Which statement about the PTIN and the EFIN is correct?
options: They are the same number
The PTIN identifies an individual preparer and carries a fee; the EFIN identifies an e-file provider, may go to a firm, and is free
The EFIN is issued only to individuals
The EFIN replaces the PTIN on e-filed returns
questions.explanation: The PTIN goes in the paid-preparer block; the EFIN accompanies electronic return data. Most preparers need both.
questions.pageTitle: PTIN requirements

questions.stem: A firm principal takes no steps to adopt compliance procedures, and one employee makes a single error on one return. Is § 10.36 engaged?
options: Yes, the absence of procedures is itself the violation
No, because each ground requires a pattern or practice of noncompliance
Yes, if the error caused an understatement
No, unless the principal is a partner
questions.explanation: Sections 10.36(b)(1), (2) and (3) each require that firm members, associates or employees are, or have been, engaged in a pattern or practice of failing to comply.
questions.pageTitle: Practitioner supervisory responsibilities (Circular 230)

questions.stem: Which ground applies where adequate procedures exist but the supervisor took no reasonable steps to ensure they were followed?
options: None; procedures on paper satisfy the section
questions.explanation: Section 10.36(b)(1) addresses the failure to ensure adequate procedures exist; (b)(2) addresses the failure to ensure procedures in effect are properly followed.
questions.pageTitle: Practitioner supervisory responsibilities (Circular 230)

questions.stem: What mental state must be shown under § 10.36(b)?
options: Negligence
Simple failure to supervise
Wilfulness, recklessness, or gross incompetence
Wilfulness only
questions.explanation: All three grounds use the same formula, and § 10.52(a)(2) names § 10.36 among the sections sanctionable on recklessness or gross incompetence without wilfulness.
questions.pageTitle: Practitioner supervisory responsibilities (Circular 230)

questions.stem: A firm has never designated anyone as responsible for Circular 230 compliance. What follows?
options: Section 10.36 does not apply to the firm
The most senior partner is automatically responsible
The IRS may identify one or more individuals subject to Part 10 as responsible
Responsibility falls on whoever signs the most returns
questions.explanation: Section 10.36(a) provides that in the absence of a person identified by the firm, the IRS may identify one or more individuals subject to Part 10.
questions.pageTitle: Practitioner supervisory responsibilities (Circular 230)

questions.stem: A principal learns in March of a pattern of noncompliance and acts on it in August, having deferred it for the filing season. Which ground is in play?
options: None, because she eventually acted
questions.explanation: Section 10.36(b)(3) covers an individual who knows or should know of the pattern and, through wilfulness, recklessness or gross incompetence, fails to take prompt action to correct it. Eventual action is not prompt action.
questions.pageTitle: Practitioner supervisory responsibilities (Circular 230)

questions.stem: A practitioner is suspended from practice by their state accountancy board. Under Circular 230 this is:
options: Irrelevant, since the state has no authority over IRS practice
Disreputable conduct under § 10.51(a)(10) in its own right
Sanctionable only if the underlying conduct involved federal tax
Grounds for automatic disbarment
questions.explanation: Discipline by a state authority, a federal court of record or a federal agency is itself listed conduct.
questions.pageTitle: Incompetence and disreputable conduct that may result in a disciplinary proceeding

questions.stem: Which provision allows sanction without a finding of willfulness?
options: Section 10.52(a)(1), for violating any regulation in the part
Section 10.52(a)(2), for violating §§ 10.34, 10.35, 10.36 or 10.37 recklessly or through gross incompetence
Section 10.51(a)(6), failure to file
None; Circular 230 always requires willfulness
questions.pageTitle: Incompetence and disreputable conduct that may result in a disciplinary proceeding

questions.stem: A member of the public telephones the IRS to allege a practitioner falsified a client's records. Under § 10.53:
options: Nothing happens unless the report is put in writing by the caller
The IRS employee receiving it must make a written report and submit it
The report may only come from an IRS employee
The allegation must first go to the practitioner
questions.explanation: Section 10.53(b) allows an oral report from a person other than an IRS employee; the employee reduces it to writing.
questions.pageTitle: Incompetence and disreputable conduct that may result in a disciplinary proceeding

questions.stem: A practitioner's conduct fits none of the eighteen categories in § 10.51(a). It follows that:
options: The conduct cannot be disreputable
The conduct may still be disreputable, the list being non-exhaustive
Only § 10.52 can apply
A proceeding requires a criminal conviction first
questions.pageTitle: Incompetence and disreputable conduct that may result in a disciplinary proceeding

questions.stem: An enrolled agent collects funds from a client to pay a tax liability and remits them three weeks late, the client suffering no loss. This is:
options: Outside § 10.51 because nothing was misappropriated
Within § 10.51(a)(8), which covers failure to remit promptly as well as misappropriation
Sanctionable only under § 10.52
A matter for the state board rather than OPR
questions.pageTitle: Incompetence and disreputable conduct that may result in a disciplinary proceeding

questions.stem: OPR seeks a nine-month suspension. The allegations of fact necessary to a finding against the practitioner must be proven:
options: By a preponderance of the evidence
By clear and convincing evidence
Beyond a reasonable doubt
By substantial evidence
questions.explanation: Section 10.76(b) applies the clear and convincing standard to suspensions of six months or longer.
questions.pageTitle: Sanctions imposed by the Office of Professional Responsibility

questions.stem: The maximum monetary penalty under Circular 230 is:
options: $5,000 per violation
The gross income derived, or to be derived, from the conduct giving rise to the penalty
50 percent of the fee
Set annually by revenue procedure
questions.explanation: Section 10.50(c)(2).
questions.pageTitle: Sanctions imposed by the Office of Professional Responsibility

questions.stem: A practitioner is censured. The practitioner:
options: May not practise before the IRS until reinstated
May continue to practise, subject to conditions the IRS may impose
Is suspended for six months automatically
Must re-sit the enrolled agent examination
questions.explanation: Sections 10.79(c) and 10.79(d).
questions.pageTitle: Sanctions imposed by the Office of Professional Responsibility

questions.stem: Which is true of a reprimand under § 10.60(a)?
options: It is the same as censure and is published
It is an alternative to instituting a proceeding and is not a § 10.50 sanction
It requires an Administrative Law Judge decision
It bars practice for one year
questions.pageTitle: Sanctions imposed by the Office of Professional Responsibility

questions.stem: A practitioner is disbarred. The earliest a petition for reinstatement may be made is:
options: Immediately
One year later
Five years later
Never
questions.explanation: Section 10.81(a); the shorter-period alternative applies to suspension and disqualification, not disbarment.
questions.pageTitle: Sanctions imposed by the Office of Professional Responsibility

questions.stem: Which of the following is a "specified submission" for IRC 6702(b)?
options: An amended return on Form 1040-X
A request for a collection due process hearing under § 6330
A protest to Appeals following a 30-day letter
A Form 843 claim for refund
questions.explanation: The definition covers § 6320 and § 6330 hearing requests and applications under §§ 6159, 7122 and 7811.
questions.pageTitle: Frivolous submissions (returns and documents)

questions.stem: A taxpayer files a return reporting wages accurately but claiming a deduction a court later rejects as untenable. The IRC 6702 penalty:
options: Applies, because the position was rejected
Does not apply, because the return permits the self-assessment to be judged and the position is not listed
Applies at half the usual amount
Applies only if the taxpayer is represented
questions.pageTitle: Frivolous submissions (returns and documents)

questions.stem: The IRS notifies a taxpayer that his installment agreement application is a specified frivolous submission. To avoid the penalty he must:
options: Pay the tax in full within 30 days
Withdraw the submission within 30 days of the notice
Request a CDP hearing
Nothing; the penalty is already fixed
questions.pageTitle: Frivolous submissions (returns and documents)

questions.stem: A client's return strikes out the penalty-of-perjury declaration above the signature line. This is:
options: A harmless formality
A listed frivolous position under Notice 2010-33, with failure-to-file exposure alongside
Only a Circular 230 matter
Grounds for the accuracy-related penalty alone
questions.pageTitle: Frivolous submissions (returns and documents)

questions.stem: A practitioner files a return advancing a listed frivolous position at the client's insistence, disclosing it on Form 8275. The practitioner:
options: Is protected, disclosure having been made
Faces Circular 230 § 10.34(b) exposure and, on willfulness, § 10.51(a)(7), disclosure being irrelevant to a frivolous position
Faces no exposure, the position being the client's
Must file but should resign afterwards
questions.pageTitle: Frivolous submissions (returns and documents)

questions.stem: An examiner finds unexplained increases in a taxpayer's net worth over four years. Standing alone, this is:
options: An affirmative act of fraud
An indicator of fraud, which does not by itself establish that any action was taken
Conclusive of intent to evade
Irrelevant to a fraud determination
questions.pageTitle: Fraudulent transactions (e.g., badges of fraud)

questions.stem: In a civil fraud case the government must prove fraud:
options: By a preponderance of the evidence
By clear and convincing evidence
Beyond a reasonable doubt
By substantial evidence
questions.explanation: Beyond a reasonable doubt is the criminal standard.
questions.pageTitle: Fraudulent transactions (e.g., badges of fraud)

questions.stem: The Secretary establishes that one item of a $200,000 underpayment is fraudulent. Under IRC 6663(b):
options: Only that item carries the penalty
The entire underpayment is treated as fraudulent unless the taxpayer establishes otherwise by a preponderance
The penalty is prorated automatically
The penalty applies only if the fraudulent item exceeds half the underpayment
questions.pageTitle: Fraudulent transactions (e.g., badges of fraud)

questions.stem: A taxpayer restructures a transaction in advance, disclosing everything, to fall within a favourable provision. This is:
options: Evasion, because the purpose was to reduce tax
Avoidance, which is lawful, there being no concealment or misrepresentation
A frivolous position
An affirmative act of fraud
questions.pageTitle: Fraudulent transactions (e.g., badges of fraud)

questions.stem: A preparer discovers that a client's prior-year return omitted income. Circular 230 requires the practitioner to:
options: File an amended return immediately
Advise the client promptly of the noncompliance and its consequences
Notify the IRS
Withdraw from the engagement without explanation
questions.explanation: Section 10.21 is an obligation to inform the client, not the IRS.
questions.pageTitle: Fraudulent transactions (e.g., badges of fraud)

questions.stem: A preparer disagrees with a proposed § 6694(a) penalty. Which forum hears the merits if the dispute is not resolved administratively?
options: The United States Tax Court
A United States district court, on a refund suit
The Office of Professional Responsibility
The Court of Federal Claims only
questions.explanation: Section 6696(b) switches off deficiency procedures, so there is no Tax Court petition.
questions.pageTitle: Assessment and appeal procedures for preparer penalties

questions.stem: To stop collection while contesting an assessed § 6694 penalty, the preparer must pay:
options: The full amount
15 percent, within 30 days of notice and demand, with a claim for refund
20 percent, within 60 days
Nothing, if an appeal is pending
questions.pageTitle: Assessment and appeal procedures for preparer penalties

questions.stem: A preparer files a claim for refund on 1 March and hears nothing. The deadline to begin the district court proceeding is:
options: 30 days after the claim is eventually denied, whenever that is
30 days after 1 September
Two years after 1 March
There is no deadline while the claim is open
questions.explanation: The period runs from the earlier of denial or six months after filing.
questions.pageTitle: Assessment and appeal procedures for preparer penalties

questions.stem: A § 6695 penalty relates to a return filed on 15 April 2023. The client signed a Form 872 extending their own assessment period. On 1 September 2026 the IRS proposes the penalty. It is:
options: Timely, because the Form 872 extended both periods
Timely, because § 6695 has no limitation period
Time-barred, because the three-year period ran and only a Form 872-D would extend it
Timely, because the penalty period runs from assessment
questions.pageTitle: Assessment and appeal procedures for preparer penalties

questions.stem: A final judicial decision establishes there was no understatement on the return underlying a § 6694 penalty the preparer paid five years ago. The preparer:
options: Has no remedy, the refund period having closed
May claim abatement and refund on Form 6118 without regard to any limitation period
Must first obtain the client's consent
May recover only if a pre-assessment appeal was taken
questions.pageTitle: Assessment and appeal procedures for preparer penalties

questions.stem: A preparer takes an undisclosed position with no substantial authority, earning a $12,000 fee, and an understatement results. The § 6694(a) penalty is:
options: The statutory floor
$6,000, being 50 percent of the income derived
75 percent of the fee
questions.explanation: The penalty is the greater of the floor or 50 percent of income derived.
questions.pageTitle: Types of penalties a preparer faces

questions.stem: Which § 6695 penalty has no annual maximum?
options: Failure to sign the return
Failure to furnish a copy to the taxpayer
Negotiation of a taxpayer's refund check
Failure to retain a copy or list
questions.explanation: Check negotiation and the due diligence penalty are uncapped.
questions.pageTitle: Types of penalties a preparer faces

questions.stem: A return claims head of household status, the child tax credit, and the earned income credit, with no due diligence performed on any. The § 6695(g) exposure is:
options: One penalty, because it is one return
Three penalties, one per eligibility determination
One penalty capped annually
No penalty if the return is accurate
questions.explanation: The penalty applies per failure.
questions.pageTitle: Types of penalties a preparer faces

questions.stem: A bookkeeper knowingly supplies fabricated figures used on a client's return. The bookkeeper does not sign the return and is not paid for tax work. Which penalty applies?
options: None, because the bookkeeper is not a return preparer
IRC § 6694(b), for reckless conduct
IRC § 6701, for aiding and abetting an understatement
IRC § 6695(b), for failure to sign
questions.explanation: Section 6701 requires neither preparer status, a signature, nor compensation.
questions.pageTitle: Types of penalties a preparer faces

questions.stem: A preparer carelessly, but not knowingly, uses a client's return information to market an unrelated service. The exposure is:
options: A misdemeanor under IRC § 7216
The civil penalty under IRC § 6713
Both, since the acts are identical
Neither, because marketing is not disclosure
questions.explanation: Section 7216 needs knowing or reckless conduct; § 6713 does not.
questions.pageTitle: Types of penalties a preparer faces

questions.stem: A preparer must furnish the taxpayer a completed copy of the return:
options: Within 30 days of filing
Not later than the time the return is presented for the taxpayer's signature
Before the return's due date
On request only
questions.pageTitle: Furnishing a copy of a return to a taxpayer

questions.stem: For an electronically filed return, a complete copy consists of:
options: A printed Form 1040 facsimile
The electronic portion filed with the IRS, including all schedules, forms, PDF attachments and jurats
A client summary showing the refund or balance
Whatever the taxpayer requests
questions.pageTitle: Furnishing a copy of a return to a taxpayer

questions.stem: May the copy given to the taxpayer omit the preparer's identifying number?
options: No, it must mirror the filed return exactly
Yes, the regulation says so expressly
Only for paper returns
Only with the taxpayer's written consent
questions.pageTitle: Furnishing a copy of a return to a taxpayer

questions.stem: A preparer delivers all client copies by secure portal without asking. A client who wanted paper complains. The preparer:
options: Is compliant, electronic delivery being permitted
Is not compliant as to that client, since the media must be acceptable to both parties
Is not compliant as to any client
Must deliver on paper in every case
questions.pageTitle: Furnishing a copy of a return to a taxpayer

questions.stem: The § 6695(a) penalty does not apply where the failure is:
options: Unintentional
Due to reasonable cause and not due to willful neglect, substantiated in writing
Corrected within 30 days
Caused by software
questions.explanation: Reasonable cause is cause arising despite ordinary care and prudence.
questions.pageTitle: Furnishing a copy of a return to a taxpayer

questions.stem: For a paper return, the signing tax return preparer must sign:
options: After the taxpayer signs
After the return is completed and before it is presented to the taxpayer for signature
At any time before filing
Only if the taxpayer requests it
questions.pageTitle: Signing returns and furnishing identifying numbers

questions.stem: The assigned preparer is unavailable. Another preparer may sign:
options: Immediately, as a matter of firm convenience
After reviewing the entire preparation of the return
Only with the taxpayer's written consent
Never; the return must wait
questions.pageTitle: Signing returns and furnishing identifying numbers

questions.stem: A preparer employed by a firm prepares a client's return. The filed return must carry:
options: The preparer's PTIN only
The preparer's PTIN and the firm's EIN
The firm's EIN only
The preparer's social security number
questions.pageTitle: Signing returns and furnishing identifying numbers

questions.stem: A single return is filed unsigned and without any preparer identifying number. The exposure is:
options: One penalty, the failures being related
Two separate penalties under § 6695(b) and § 6695(c), each with its own annual cap
A single penalty at double the rate
No penalty absent willfulness
questions.pageTitle: Signing returns and furnishing identifying numbers

questions.stem: For an electronically signed return, the preparer must:
options: Sign before presenting the copy, as for paper
Furnish all information to be transmitted contemporaneously with the Form 8879, then sign electronically
Sign only after the IRS accepts the return
Obtain a paper signature as well
questions.pageTitle: Signing returns and furnishing identifying numbers

questions.stem: A preparer choosing the list option rather than retaining copies must record, for each return:
options: The taxpayer's name and identifying number
The name, identifying number, taxable year, and type of return or claim
The full return as filed
Only the taxable year
questions.pageTitle: Keeping copies or lists of returns prepared

questions.stem: A return period for these purposes is:
options: The calendar year
The 12-month period beginning 1 July
The taxpayer's taxable year
The filing season
questions.pageTitle: Keeping copies or lists of returns prepared

questions.stem: A return is presented for signature in June 2026 and, with extensions, becomes due in December 2026. Records must be retained until:
options: Three years after June 2026
Three years after the close of the return period ending 30 June 2027
Three years after filing
Six years after presentation
questions.explanation: The return became due during the later return period.
questions.pageTitle: Keeping copies or lists of returns prepared

questions.stem: A partnership that prepared returns dissolves before the retention period expires. The obligation:
options: Ends with the partnership
Passes to those responsible under state law for winding up, or failing that to the general partners collectively
Passes to the successor firm only
Passes to the clients
questions.pageTitle: Keeping copies or lists of returns prepared

questions.stem: The maximum penalty under IRC 6695(d) is measured:
options: Per calendar year
Per return period
Per taxpayer
There is no maximum
questions.explanation: unlike the calendar-year caps in § 6695(a) to (c).
questions.pageTitle: Keeping copies or lists of returns prepared

questions.stem: Under the current regulation, a person employing signing tax return preparers must:
options: File an information return by 31 July following the return period
Retain a record of each preparer and make it available for inspection on request
File Form 8867 for each preparer
Register each preparer with the IRS
questions.explanation: Reg. § 1.6060-1(a)(1), under the alternative authorised by IRC § 6060(b).
questions.pageTitle: Employees engaged or employed during a return period (e.g. IRC Section 6060)

questions.stem: The record must show, for each preparer:
options: Name only
Name, identifying number and principal place of work
Name and salary
Name and the returns prepared
questions.pageTitle: Employees engaged or employed during a return period (e.g. IRC Section 6060)

questions.stem: An enrolled agent practising alone and employing nobody:
options: Is outside § 6060
Is treated as his own employer and must keep a record about himself
Must file the 31 July return the statute describes
Is covered only if he signs more than 10 returns
questions.pageTitle: Employees engaged or employed during a return period (e.g. IRC Section 6060)

questions.stem: A firm produces its payroll register, which lists all employees without indicating who prepared returns. This:
options: Satisfies the regulation, any documentation being acceptable
Fails, because the record must disclose on its face which individuals were preparers
Satisfies it if the firm explains verbally
Fails only if the IRS cannot identify them at all
questions.pageTitle: Employees engaged or employed during a return period (e.g. IRC Section 6060)

questions.stem: The maximum penalty under IRC 6695(e) is measured:
options: Per calendar year
Per return period
Per preparer
Per return prepared
questions.pageTitle: Employees engaged or employed during a return period (e.g. IRC Section 6060)

questions.stem: A return claims head of household status, the EIC and the CTC, with due diligence failed on all three. The number of IRC 6695(g) penalties is:
options: One, because it is one return
Three, one per determination
One, capped annually
Two, filing status not counting
questions.pageTitle: Preparer due diligence and penalties (e.g., refundable credits, head of household status)

questions.stem: A nonsigning tax return preparer satisfies the Form 8867 requirement by:
options: Filing it with the IRS directly
Providing the completed form to the signing preparer for inclusion with the filed return
Retaining it in the file
Nothing; the duty falls on the signer alone
questions.pageTitle: Preparer due diligence and penalties (e.g., refundable credits, head of household status)

questions.stem: A preparer telephones a client to resolve an apparent inconsistency, is satisfied, and files. No note is made. The knowledge requirement is:
options: Satisfied, the inquiry having been made
Not satisfied, because inquiries and responses must be contemporaneously documented
Satisfied if the answer was correct
Inapplicable to telephone inquiries
questions.pageTitle: Preparer due diligence and penalties (e.g., refundable credits, head of household status)

questions.stem: The exception in Reg. 1.6695-2(d) requires the preparer to show:
options: Reasonable cause
Both that normal office procedures are reasonably designed and routinely followed, and that the failure was isolated and inadvertent
That the client misled the preparer
That the credit was ultimately allowable
questions.explanation: and it is unavailable to a firm penalised under the firm rule.
questions.pageTitle: Preparer due diligence and penalties (e.g., refundable credits, head of household status)

questions.stem: A firm employing a penalised preparer is itself liable:
options: Automatically
Only if management participated or knew, the firm failed to establish reasonable procedures, or it disregarded its own procedures through willfulness, recklessness or gross indifference
Only if it is a partnership
Never
questions.pageTitle: Preparer due diligence and penalties (e.g., refundable credits, head of household status)

questions.stem: Which is NOT a required element of a power of attorney under Reg. § 601.503(a)?
options: The taxpayer's identification number
A description of the matters for which representation is authorized
The representative's Centralized Authorization File number
A clear expression of the taxpayer's intention as to the scope of authority
questions.explanation: The six elements do not include a CAF number; the CAF is how the authorization is processed, not what makes it valid.
questions.pageTitle: Purpose of a power of attorney before the IRS

questions.stem: A properly completed Form 2848 serves as:
options: A power of attorney only
A tax information authorization only
Both a power of attorney and a declaration of representative
A substitute for eligibility under Circular 230
questions.explanation: Reg. § 601.503(b)(1) says it satisfies both § 601.503(a) and § 601.502(c).
questions.pageTitle: Purpose of a power of attorney before the IRS

questions.stem: A taxpayer signs Form 8821 naming her accountant. The accountant may:
options: Represent her at an examination
Inspect and receive her confidential tax information for the listed matters and periods
Sign a consent extending the assessment period
Argue an appeal on her behalf
questions.explanation: A tax information authorization confers access to information and no authority to act.
questions.pageTitle: Purpose of a power of attorney before the IRS

questions.stem: A Form 2848 describes "Income, Form 1040, 2024." The revenue agent wants to discuss 2023. The representative may:
options: Discuss 2023, because it is the same taxpayer and the same tax
Discuss 2023 only if it affects 2024
Not discuss 2023 without a power of attorney covering it
Discuss 2023 if the taxpayer consents orally
questions.explanation: Authority is bounded by the description of matters, and 2023 is outside it.
questions.pageTitle: Purpose of a power of attorney before the IRS

questions.stem: A representative holds a Form 2848 authorising representation for a year under examination, with no additional acts stated. May she sign a consent extending the assessment period?
options: Yes, it is incidental to representation
Yes, if the examiner requests it
No — authority to sign a consent must be expressly granted
Yes, if she notifies the client afterwards
questions.explanation: Binding the taxpayer requires authority within the taxpayer's expressed scope.
questions.pageTitle: Signature authority: consents, closing agreements, and refund checks

questions.stem: A consent extending the assessment period is signed two weeks after the original period expired. Its effect is:
options: It revives the period
It extends the period from the date signed
None — there was no open period to extend
It extends the period only for issues under examination
questions.explanation: Section 6501(c)(4)(A) requires the consent before the prescribed time expires.
questions.pageTitle: Signature authority: consents, closing agreements, and refund checks

questions.stem: A closing agreement approved by the Secretary may be reopened:
options: At the taxpayer's request within two years
Only on a showing of fraud, malfeasance, or misrepresentation of a material fact
Whenever new evidence emerges
Never, in any circumstances
questions.explanation: Those are the exceptions to finality in IRC § 7121(b).
questions.pageTitle: Signature authority: consents, closing agreements, and refund checks

questions.stem: Which is permitted under Circular 230 § 10.31?
options: Endorsing a client's refund check to collect a fee
Having the client's refund deposited into the firm's account and remitting the balance
Receiving the client's refund check and giving it to the client
Accepting an electronic refund payment into an account the practitioner controls
questions.explanation: Receiving is not negotiating; the other three are what the section prohibits.
questions.pageTitle: Signature authority: consents, closing agreements, and refund checks

questions.stem: A taxpayer signs a new Form 2848 naming a second representative for the same year, saying nothing about the first. The effect on the first authorization is:
options: Both remain in force
The new one revokes it
Both are void for conflict
The first remains until the taxpayer files a statement of revocation
questions.explanation: Reg. § 601.505(a)(1) revokes the prior authority for the same matter unless the new document says otherwise and carries the required attachment.
questions.pageTitle: Authority granted by the taxpayer, and its boundaries

questions.stem: Which act does NOT come with an ordinary grant of representation authority?
options: Receiving and inspecting confidential tax information for the listed periods
Signing a consent extending the assessment period
Attending a conference with the IRS
Corresponding with the IRS about the matter
questions.explanation: Binding the taxpayer by consent must be authorised expressly.
questions.pageTitle: Authority granted by the taxpayer, and its boundaries

questions.stem: A practitioner will handle a matter entirely by letter. He must:
options: File nothing, since no appearance is contemplated
File Form 8821 only
Submit a power of attorney and declaration of representative
Obtain the examiner's permission
questions.explanation: Reg. § 601.504(d) requires it even where no personal appearance is contemplated.
questions.pageTitle: Authority granted by the taxpayer, and its boundaries

questions.stem: A client instructs her practitioner in writing to have her refund deposited into the firm's account, net of fees. The practitioner may:
options: Do so, because the client instructed it in writing
Do so if the client is told the amount first
Not do so — Circular 230 § 10.31(a) prohibits it regardless of the client's consent
Do so if the firm holds it in trust
questions.explanation: The prohibition runs against the practitioner and is not the client's to waive.
questions.pageTitle: Authority granted by the taxpayer, and its boundaries

questions.stem: Which is NOT a circumstance in which an agent may make a taxpayer's return?
options: The taxpayer cannot make it by reason of disease or injury
The taxpayer has been continuously outside the United States for at least 60 days before the prescribed filing date
The taxpayer is travelling for work and finds it inconvenient to sign
The district director determines good cause exists after a written request
questions.explanation: Inconvenience is not a ground; the three circumstances in Reg. § 1.6012-1(a)(5) are exhaustive.
questions.pageTitle: Limitations on signing a tax return for a taxpayer

questions.stem: When an agent makes a return under Reg. § 1.6012-1(a)(5), the return must be accompanied by:
options: Nothing further
A power of attorney authorising the agent to make, execute, or file it
Form 8821
A statement of the agent's credentials
questions.explanation: A properly completed Form 2848 is sufficient for the purpose.
questions.pageTitle: Limitations on signing a tax return for a taxpayer

questions.stem: A wife signs a joint return for her husband, who cannot sign because of injury and who consented orally. What must she attach?
options: Nothing, because consent was oral
A power of attorney
A dated statement she has signed giving the return name, the taxable year, the reason he cannot sign, and that he consented
A physician's certificate
questions.explanation: The regulation requires exactly those four elements in an attached, signed, dated statement.
questions.pageTitle: Limitations on signing a tax return for a taxpayer

questions.stem: An agent signs a client's return under a valid authority, and the return understates tax. Who is exposed to penalties?
options: The taxpayer only
The agent only
Both the taxpayer and the agent
Neither, because the authority was valid
questions.explanation: The regulation makes the taxpayer and the agent responsible for the return as made.
questions.pageTitle: Limitations on signing a tax return for a taxpayer

questions.stem: A Form 2848 lists "Income, 1040, All years" on line 3. What happens?
options: The IRS records it for all open years
The IRS narrows it to the current year
The IRS returns the power of attorney
The IRS records it but limits it to three years
questions.explanation: The instructions state that the IRS will return any power of attorney with a general reference such as "All years," "All periods," or "All taxes."
questions.pageTitle: Proper completion of power of attorney (Form 2848)

questions.stem: Which act does a Form 2848 grant without any box being checked on line 5a?
options: Consenting to disclosure of the return to a third party
Signing the taxpayer's income tax return
Substituting another representative
None of these — each requires an express authorisation
questions.explanation: Each of the line 5a acts, including Intermediate Service Provider access, must be specifically authorised by the taxpayer.
questions.pageTitle: Proper completion of power of attorney (Form 2848)

questions.stem: On which ground may an agent sign an individual income tax return under Reg. § 1.6012-1(a)(5)?
options: The taxpayer is travelling for work
Continuous absence from the United States for at least 60 days before the due date
The taxpayer has authorised it in writing
The representative holds a valid PTIN
questions.explanation: The three grounds are disease or injury, continuous absence from the United States including Puerto Rico for at least 60 days before the due date, or specific IRS permission for other good cause.
questions.pageTitle: Proper completion of power of attorney (Form 2848)

questions.stem: A married couple filed jointly and both sign one Form 2848 naming one enrolled agent. Effect?
options: Both spouses are represented
Only one is; each must execute a separate Form 2848
The form is invalid
Both are, if the agent countersigns
questions.explanation: The instructions require each spouse to execute his or her own power of attorney on a separate Form 2848.
questions.pageTitle: Proper completion of power of attorney (Form 2848)

questions.stem: What does an unenrolled return preparer enter in Part II under designation (h)?
options: A state bar number
An enrollment card number
A valid PTIN
A CAF number
questions.explanation: The instructions state that unenrolled return preparers must possess a valid PTIN to represent a taxpayer before the IRS.
questions.pageTitle: Proper completion of power of attorney (Form 2848)

questions.stem: A non-IRS power of attorney satisfies every requirement of Reg. § 601.503(a). What else is needed to get it recorded on the CAF?
options: Nothing further
A completed Form 2848 attached, signed by the representative but not the taxpayer
A completed Form 2848 signed by the taxpayer
A court order
questions.explanation: Reg. § 601.503(b)(2) — the attached Form 2848 is not the operative power of attorney and need not be signed by the taxpayer, but the Declaration of Representative must be signed by the representative.
questions.pageTitle: Alternate forms of power of attorney (durable)

questions.stem: What is required before an attorney-in-fact may perfect a defective non-IRS power of attorney?
options: The taxpayer must countersign the Form 2848
The attorney-in-fact must be eligible to practise
The original must contemplate authorization to handle federal tax matters
The original must be recorded with a court
questions.explanation: Reg. § 601.503(b)(3) requires that, plus a statement under penalty of perjury that the original is valid under the laws of the governing jurisdiction.
questions.pageTitle: Alternate forms of power of attorney (durable)

questions.stem: How does Reg. § 601.501(b)(9)(ii) define a durable power of attorney?
options: One with no stated expiry date
One whose appointment does not end by passage of time or by the principal's incompetency
One authorising any and all acts
One filed with a court
questions.explanation: Authority continues until the taxpayer's death and survives incompetency. Whether it operates before the IRS is a separate question — see Pub. 947 on incapacity.
questions.pageTitle: Alternate forms of power of attorney (durable)

questions.stem: What happens to a power of attorney before the IRS when the taxpayer becomes incompetent?
options: It continues automatically
Generally terminated, unless line 5a authorises continuation and an acceptable non-IRS durable power exists
It continues if the representative is an enrolled agent
It becomes a tax information authorization
questions.explanation: Pub. 947 states a power of attorney is generally terminated on incapacity or incompetency, and gives both conditions for it to continue.
questions.pageTitle: Alternate forms of power of attorney (durable)

questions.stem: An attorney-in-fact who cannot practise perfects a durable power. Who may be named representative?
options: The attorney-in-fact, the perfection having cured the document
Nobody; the taxpayer must sign a new form
An individual who can practise before the IRS, who signs the declaration
The court-appointed guardian
questions.explanation: Perfecting the document confers no eligibility; only an individual described in Reg. § 601.502(b) can make the declaration.
questions.pageTitle: Alternate forms of power of attorney (durable)

questions.stem: One written consent authorises a preparer both to use client data for marketing and to disclose it to a lender. Valid?
options: Yes, if both are specifically identified
Yes, for Form 1040 series filers
No, one document cannot authorise both uses and disclosures
Yes, if the taxpayer receives a copy
questions.explanation: Reg. § 301.7216-3(c)(1) requires one document for uses and a separate one for disclosures, each specifically and separately identifying every use or disclosure.
questions.pageTitle: Rules for client privacy and consent to disclose

questions.stem: A preparer will not prepare a return unless the client consents to marketing for the firm's insurance products. Effect?
options: Valid if signed and dated
Involuntary, and it fails
Valid but limited to one year
Valid if a copy is given to the client
questions.explanation: Conditioning any services on furnishing consent makes it involuntary under Reg. § 301.7216-3(a)(1). The only exception is consent to disclose to another preparer assisting with that taxpayer's return.
questions.pageTitle: Rules for client privacy and consent to disclose

questions.stem: A taxpayer signs a § 6103(c) consent on 1 April. By when must the IRS receive it?
options: Within 30 days
Within 60 days
Within 120 days of the signature date
Before the return's due date
questions.explanation: Reg. § 301.6103(c)-1(b)(2) — no disclosure unless the consent is received within 120 days following the date the taxpayer signed and dated it.
questions.pageTitle: Rules for client privacy and consent to disclose

questions.stem: A US preparer sends Form 1040 information abroad with the client's signed consent. What must happen to the SSN?
options: It may be sent, consent having been obtained
